ethics_check.title: Ethics Approval Check
ethics_check.summary_text: All papers that appeared to involve live data collection contained an ethics approval statement.

table.text: Ethical approval was granted by the psychology department's ethics committee at (information removed for double-blind peer review), and all procedures were compliant with the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR).
After registering for the study, participants took part in an introductory session led by trained recruiters.

If participants are instructed to change their smartphone usage in a time window too close to participants' typical shuteye time, on some evenings they may already have stopped using their smartphones simply because they are preparing for sleep, instead than in response to the manipulation.

Based on the following text, we would expect an ethics approval statement, and it was present:

> After registering for the study, participants took part in an introductory session led by trained recruiters.

power.title: Power Analysis Check
report: No power analyses were detected.

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

prereg_check.title: Preregistration Check

table.title: Within-Person Associations Between Objectively Measured Pre-Bedtime Smartphone Usage and Sleep
table.research_questions: Pre-bedtime smartphone usage is associated with a) later bedtimes, b) longer sleep onset latency, c) more difficulties to fall asleep, d) shorter sleep duration, and e) worse sleep quality.
table.study_type: Observational Study - Data is collected from study subjects that are not randomly assigned to a treatment. This includes surveys, “natural experiments,” and regression discontinuity designs.
table.blinding: No blinding is involved in this study.
table.study_design_overview:
Daily diary study 
For a period of 10 days, participants reported when they fell asleep, how long it took them to fall asleep, how difficult it was to fall asleep, how well they slept in the previous night, and at what time they woke up on the respective day. In addition, a smartphone sensing app continuously logged their smartphone usage during this period.
table.existing_data: Registration prior to analysis of the data
table.existing_data_explanation:
We will use data collected in the "eMotion Study: Couples’ Everyday Life in a Digitalized World". The data collection is ongoing and we will use all data that has been collected up until now.  All predictor variables require preprocessing of the smartphone data and have not been extracted prior to this pre-registration. 

In respect to the sleep data, self-reported sleep onset and wake-up time have been used for data cleaning purposes (e.g., correct for "time asleep" in a project looking at active shared couple time), but have not been investigated as outcome variables.
table.data_collection_procedures:
Recruitment: 
Study participants (goal: N = 200 couples, n = 400 individuals) are recruited via online advertisements on the social media platforms “Facebook”, “WhatsApp”, and “Instagram”, as well as via mailing lists, (local) newspapers, and via radio podcasts. In addition, attention is drawn to the study within counseling centers for couples and families. 

Eligibility: 
- The participants must be at least 18 years old
- The participants are in a stable romantic relationship of at least six months
- Partners live together
- Both partners need to be willing to participate
- Both partners need to own a smartphone 
-  At least one partner owns a smartphone with the Android operating system and at least Android version 7
- The study participants are willing to download the app movisensXS and it runs on at least one of the smartphones
- Sufficient German language proficiency

Remuneration: 
Daily diary:
Participants receive up to 48 Euros per person for their participation in the daily diary part: The participants will receive 8€ for filling out the (pre/post) questionnaire. Additionally, they will receive 0,50 € per ‘beeped’ questionnaire that they fill out (6 per day). By answering at least 80% of the smartphone signals, participants receive an additional bonus payment of 10€. This form of additional remuneration to increase compliance is a common practice. 

Alternatively, (psychology) students can opt for 6 course credits. By answering at least 80% of the smartphone signals, student participants receive an additional bonus payment of 10€. 

Mobile Sensing: 
Participants receive up to 20 Euros per person: 2 Euros per day that mobile sensing data is tracked (10 x 2 Euro = 20 Euro). Alternatively, psychology students can receive 2 course credits.

Sample for this study: 
To avoid dependencies in the data, if both partners have smartphone sensing data only one partner per couple will be randomly chosen to be included in the analyses for this study.

In addition, we have the following exclusion criteria on the level of nights:
We will exclude nights: 
- with a sleep duration of less than 2 hours and more than 16 hours
- if the wake-up time is not in the interval between 4 a.m. and 3 p.m.
- if the bedtime is not in the interval between 5 p.m. and 5 a.m.

This ensures that extraordinary nights do not bias the analyses.
table.measured_variables:
Sleep outcomes: 

Difficulties to fall asleep: 

Measured with the following item: 
Wie schwer ist es Ihnen gefallen, letzte Nacht einzuschlafen?
[How difficult was it for you to fall asleep last night?]
Scale from 1 (gar nicht/not at all) to 7 (sehr/very much).

Sleep quality: 

Measured with the item: 
Wie haben Sie letzte Nacht geschlafen? 
[How did you sleep last night?]
Scale: 1 (sehr schlecht/very poorly) to 7 (sehr gut/very well)

Sleep onset latency:

Measured with the following question: 
Was schätzen Sie, wie lange haben Sie zum Einschlafen gebraucht? More Button Einschlafen: Die Zeit zwischen dem Lichtausschalten und dem Einschlafen (also die Zeit, in der Sie die Absicht hatten, einzuschlafen; nicht Lesen oder Handynutzung).
[How long do you estimate it took you to fall asleep? More Button Falling Asleep: The time between turning off the lights and falling asleep (i.e., the time when you intended to sleep; not reading or using your phone).
Items: sleepla1h, sleepla1m

We will implement the following corrections to address potential inaccuracies in the self-reports and ensure that exceptional nights do not skew the analyses: 
•	If sleep onset latency is more than 1 hour but participants indicate that it was easy to fall asleep: We assume that they probably got confused with hours/minutes. We will use the hour-data for minutes instead. 
•	If sleep onset latency is more than 1 hour but participants do not indicate that it was easy to fall asleep (score higher than 2 or no score on the variable measuring difficulties to fall asleep), we don't know what they meant to report for sleep onset latency. We will set the sleep onset latency- values to NA.

Sleep duration:

We will use the responses to these questions to calculate sleep duration. 
1.	Ich bin letzte Nacht zur folgenden Uhrzeit eingeschlafen: Bitte geben Sie die Uhrzeit getrennt in Stunden und Minuten an (z.B. Stunde 22, Minute 00 für 22:00 Uhr)
[I fell asleep at the following time last night: Please enter the time separately in hours and minutes (e.g., hour 22, minute 00 for 10:00 PM).]
Items: asleeph; asleepm
2.	Ich bin heute Morgen zur folgenden Uhrzeit aufgewacht: Bitte geben Sie die Uhrzeit getrennt in Stunden und Minuten an (z.B. Stunde 08, Minute 30 für 08:30 Uhr). More Button: Bitte wählen Sie die Uhrzeit, zu der Ihr Wecker Sie das erste Mal geweckt hat, selbst wenn Sie danach noch nicht direkt aufgestanden sind.
[I woke up at the following time this morning: Please enter the time separately in hours and minutes (e.g., hour 08, minute 30 for 8:30 AM).  
More Button: Please select the time your alarm first woke you up, even if you didn’t get up immediately afterward.]
Items: awakeh; awakem

We will implement the following corrections to address potential inaccuracies in the self-reports:
We will set sleep duration to NA if self-reported wake-up time is before self-reported sleep onset time.

Bedtime: 

We will calculate bedtime by subtracting sleep onset latency from the response to this question:
Ich bin letzte Nacht zur folgenden Uhrzeit eingeschlafen: Bitte geben Sie die Uhrzeit getrennt in Stunden und Minuten an (z.B. Stunde 22, Minute 00 für 22:00 Uhr)
[I fell asleep at the following time last night: Please enter the time separately in hours and minutes (e.g., hour 22, minute 00 for 10:00 PM).]
Items: asleeph; asleepm

We will implement the following corrections to address potential inaccuracies in the self-reports:
We will set bedtime to NA if self-reported wake-up time is before self-reported sleep onset time.

Predictors: Pre-bedtime smartphone usage
Our predictors include the duration of pre-bedtime smartphone usage across four distinct time windows, each lasting 30 minutes and covering different segments of the 2-hour interval before bedtime:
    30 minutes before bedtime
    30 minutes to 60 minutes before bedtime
    60 minutes to 90 minutes before bedtime
    90 minutes to 120 minutes before bedtime

We will use the bedtime variable (described above) to calculate these time windows for each individual and evening. Smartphone usage will be determined by calculating the time difference between pairs of screen-on and screen-off events. The total smartphone usage for each time window will be summed accordingly.

Several logging errors may occur in the data, which we will address during preprocessing. Below, we describe these errors, their potential consequences, and how we plan to handle them:

Logging Error A: Unpaired Screen Events
These occur when either a screen-on or screen-off event is missing. Since we cannot determine when the screen usage started or ended, these unpaired events are excluded from the data. While we know some screen time may be missing, the exact duration is uncertain. "Missing time" refers to the period between regular screen event pairs and the unpaired events, during which we lack reliable data.

Logging Error B: Unrealistically Long Screen Sessions
Sessions longer than 6 hours are considered highly likely to be due to logging errors. Although we cannot be absolutely certain that these sessions were incorrectly logged, they are removed from the dataset before feature extraction. Similar to Logging Error A, the precise amount of missing screen time during these long sessions is unknown. The "missing time" refers to the duration of these excluded sessions.

Logging Error C: Unrealistically Long Gaps in Data
This refers to gaps of 14 hours or more without any recorded screen activity. While we cannot be certain that these gaps are caused by logging errors rather than actual non-usage, it is probable, as the smartphone's operating system may stop logging to conserve battery. As with the other errors, we refer to the time during these long gaps as "missing time" due to the lack of reliable information.

The "missing time" caused by all three types of logging errors will be summed for each time window. If the missing time in a given interval exceeds 5 minutes, the respective predictor will be set to NA.

We will use the response to this question to determine whether a day was a working day or a non-working day: 
Wie viele Stunden haben Sie heute insgesamt gearbeitet? Tragen Sie bei Stunden 0 ein, wenn Sie nicht gearbeitet haben.
[How many hours did you work today? If you did not work, enter 0 hours.]

0 hours = not a working day
more than 0 hours = working day
table.statistical_tests:
We will use multi-level regression models to predict level-1 sleep outcomes with level-1 pre-bedtime smartphone usage (within-person effect). We will use traditional Gaussian models with the link function unless model diagnostics indicate problems (e.g. the residual distribution). In this case, we will either transform the outcome (e.g. log-transformation) or choose a more appropriate model. 

We will run separate models for each of our 4 predictor variables (prebedtime smartphone usage in the four different time windows) and for each of our five sleep outcomes (bedtime, sleep onset latency, difficulties to fall asleep, sleep duration, and sleep quality). This results in 4x5 = 20 multi-level models. 

We will center level 1 predictors around the individual mean.

We will specify random-slope models with a maximal random effects structure in order to reduce Type I error (Barr et al., 2013). In case of failures to converge, we will – as recommended- simplify the model by dropping the random slope associated with the smallest variance.
In order to examine whether the effect of pre-bedtime smartphone usage varies based on whether the nights preceded working days, we will run additional multi-level models that also include a main effect of working day as well as an interaction term of working day and pre-bedtime smartphone usage (centered within-person) in the multi-level models.
table.transformations: In order to facilitate the interpretation of the effects, we will apply a linear transformation to the outcome "sleep quality" and "difficulties to fall asleep" and convert them into “POMP-scores”, that is the “percentage of maximum possible scores” (Cohen et al., 1999). POMP-scores are on a scale from 0 – 100 and allow for an intuitive interpretation (e.g., 5 additional minutes of prebedtime smartphone usage are associated with 20% decrease in sleep quality).

Ich bin letzte Nacht zur folgenden Uhrzeit eingeschlafen: Bitte geben Sie die Uhrzeit getrennt in Stunden und Minuten an (z.B. Stunde 22, Minute 00 für 22:00 Uhr)
[I fell asleep at the following time last night: Please enter the time separately in hours and minutes (e.g., hour 22, minute 00 for 10:00 PM).]
Items: asleeph; asleepm

We will implement the following corrections to address potential inaccuracies in the self-reports:
We will set bedtime to NA if self-reported wake-up time is before self-reported sleep onset time.

Predictors: Pre-bedtime smartphone usage
Our predictors include the duration of pre-bedtime smartphone usage across four distinct time windows, each lasting 30 minutes and covering different segments of the 2-hour interval before bedtime:
    30 minutes before bedtime
    30 minutes to 60 minutes before bedtime
    60 minutes to 90 minutes before bedtime
    90 minutes to 120 minutes before bedtime

We will use the bedtime variable (described above) to calculate these time windows for each individual and evening. Smartphone usage will be determined by calculating the time difference between pairs of screen-on and screen-off events. The total smartphone usage for each time window will be summed accordingly.

Several logging errors may occur in the data, which we will address during preprocessing. Below, we describe these errors, their potential consequences, and how we plan to handle them:

Logging Error A: Unpaired Screen Events
These occur when either a screen-on or screen-off event is missing. Since we cannot determine when the screen usage started or ended, these unpaired events are excluded from the data. While we know some screen time may be missing, the exact duration is uncertain. "Missing time" refers to the period between regular screen event pairs and the unpaired events, during which we lack reliable data.

Logging Error B: Unrealistically Long Screen Sessions
Sessions longer than 6 hours are considered highly likely to be due to logging errors. Although we cannot be absolutely certain that these sessions were incorrectly logged, they are removed from the dataset before feature extraction. Similar to Logging Error A, the precise amount of missing screen time during these long sessions is unknown. The "missing time" refers to the duration of these excluded sessions.

Logging Error C: Unrealistically Long Gaps in Data
This refers to gaps of 14 hours or more without any recorded screen activity. While we cannot be certain that these gaps are caused by logging errors rather than actual non-usage, it is probable, as the smartphone's operating system may stop logging to conserve battery. As with the other errors, we refer to the time during these long gaps as "missing time" due to the lack of reliable information.

The "missing time" caused by all three types of logging errors will be summed for each time window. If the missing time in a given interval exceeds 5 minutes, the respective predictor will be set to NA.

more than 0 hours = working day
table.statistical_tests:
We will use multi-level regression models to predict level-1 sleep outcomes with level-1 pre-bedtime smartphone usage (within-person effect). We will use traditional Gaussian models with the link function unless model diagnostics indicate problems (e.g. the residual distribution). In this case, we will either transform the outcome (e.g. log-transformation) or choose a more appropriate model. 

We will run separate models for each of our 4 predictor variables (prebedtime smartphone usage in the four different time windows) and for each of our five sleep outcomes (bedtime, sleep onset latency, difficulties to fall asleep, sleep duration, and sleep quality). This results in 4x5 = 20 multi-level models. 

We will center level 1 predictors around the individual mean.

We will specify random-slope models with a maximal random effects structure in order to reduce Type I error (Barr et al., 2013). In case of failures to converge, we will – as recommended- simplify the model by dropping the random slope associated with the smallest variance.
In order to examine whether the effect of pre-bedtime smartphone usage varies based on whether the nights preceded working days, we will run additional multi-level models that also include a main effect of working day as well as an interaction term of working day and pre-bedtime smartphone usage (centered within-person) in the multi-level models.
table.transformations: In order to facilitate the interpretation of the effects, we will apply a linear transformation to the outcome "sleep quality" and "difficulties to fall asleep" and convert them into “POMP-scores”, that is the “percentage of maximum possible scores” (Cohen et al., 1999). POMP-scores are on a scale from 0 – 100 and allow for an intuitive interpretation (e.g., 5 additional minutes of prebedtime smartphone usage are associated with 20% decrease in sleep quality).

:::

This module runs automated data-quality checks (empty columns, SPSS filter variables, category casing, stray whitespace, numbers stored as text, problematic and colliding column names, mixed text encodings, personal information, spreadsheet formatting, and careless responding) on the extracted data files.
We examined 1911 columns across 4 data files.
#### Issues Identified

176 file/column combinations have at least one issue.

**About the personal-information flags.** These are pattern matches, not confirmed disclosures, and they are tuned to over-report rather than miss something. Expect false positives:

- **Column names** are matched against identifying words in English and other European languages (`email`, `telefoonnummer`, `geboortedatum`, ...). A column called `phone_number` flags whether or not it holds one, and an empty or already-anonymised column flags on its name alone.
- **Values** are matched against the shape of an identifier. An IP address pattern also matches a version string or a dotted numeric code; a card-number pattern requires both a real issuer prefix and a checksum, but a long numeric ID can still coincide.
- **Free text** is flagged when a column holds long, mostly-distinct prose — the shape open-ended answers take. Most such columns contain no names at all.

A flag means *look at this column*. Where the data is already de-identified (an `ip` column reading `Anonymized`, a `name` column the authors emptied), no action is needed.

#### Careless Responding

347 distinct respondents were flagged for **straightlining**: giving the same answer for at least 80% of the items in a multi-item scale of 5 items or more. One respondent can be flagged in several scales; the table below is **one row per person**, and the *Longest run* column gives the run that triggered the strongest flag, so you can check it against the raw data.

Of these, **57 were flagged *only* by short-scale straightlining** (a run of identical answers on a scale of 7 items or fewer). On a short, one-directional scale, answering consistently is often normal, coherent responding rather than carelessness — treat these as weak signals and inspect the actual responses before excluding anyone.
These are prompts to inspect those rows, not definitive judgements.

**What this does not cover.** Only 1 of 4 data files could be screened: the rest had no detectable multi-item scale block, or too few respondents. Even in a screened file, these checks only look at multi-item rating scales — the only place where a repeated or flat answer pattern is interpretable. Single questions, open text, demographics and any item outside a detected scale block are never examined. A respondent can therefore answer most of a survey carelessly and still not be flagged here, and finding nothing is not evidence that a dataset is free of careless responding.

**The code was run.** Each script ran in an isolated Docker container against a throwaway copy of the repository, in the run order above, with a 300-second per-script timeout. Running against current package versions: a break can reflect version drift, which argues for pinning versions.

info.title: Rethinking Smartphones and Sleep: A Fine-Grained Within-Person Analysis of Evening Smartphone Use and Sleep

text.text: Inadequate sleep is a public health concern associated with adverse health and well-being outcomes.
Evening smartphone use is frequently cited as a potential contributor, prompting widespread recommendations to avoid it.
However, rigorous evidence to support these recommendations is limited.

Using device-based smartphone use data and experience sampling data collected over 10 days, we examined within-person associations between evening smartphone use and five self-reported sleep-related outcomes: shuteye time, sleep latency, sleep duration, difficulty to fall asleep, and sleep quality.
We examined these associations in two samples (N = 184 and N = 185) to test replicability.
To investigate robustness and temporal dynamics, we assessed smartphone use across four equal-length time windows covering different segments of the evening.
Across both samples and all time windows, greater-thanusual evening smartphone use was consistently associated with earlier shuteye time.
Associations with the other sleeprelated outcomes were less consistent, with most estimates indicating no significant relationship.
Overall, our findings align with previous intensive longitudinal research that has likewise found little evidence of concerning associations between evening smartphone use and sleep.
Our results challenge the assumption that evening smartphone use is inherently harmful to sleep and underscore the need to reconsider blanket recommendations to avoid it.
Sleep is widely recognized as a fundamental pillar of physical health, cognitive functioning, and overall wellbeing (Ramar et al., 2021).
text.formatted: Sleep is widely recognized as a fundamental pillar of physical health, cognitive functioning, and overall wellbeing <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">(Ramar et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: Nevertheless, insufficient sleep remains highly prevalent: recent estimates suggest that approximately one third of adults in Europe and North America fail to achieve the recommended 7-9 hours of sleep per night (Scott et al., 2024).
text.formatted: Nevertheless, insufficient sleep remains highly prevalent: recent estimates suggest that approximately one third of adults in Europe and North America fail to achieve the recommended 7-9 hours of sleep per night <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">(Scott et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Sleep is shaped by a complex interplay of biological, psychological, behavioral, societal, and health-related factors.
These range from social demands and structural influences, such as work schedules, to individual-level behaviors and habits (Philippens et al., 2022).
text.formatted: These range from social demands and structural influences, such as work schedules, to individual-level behaviors and habits <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">(Philippens et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: Among the latter, evening smartphone use -both ubiquitous and, in principle, readily modifiable -has received considerable attention.
Recommendations to refrain from smartphone use in the evening are widespread and frequently incorporated into sleep hygiene recommendations (Hale et al., 2018; Schuh, 2022).
text.formatted: Recommendations to refrain from smartphone use in the evening are widespread and frequently incorporated into sleep hygiene recommendations <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">(Hale et al., 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b39">Schuh, 2022)</ref>.

text.text: However, the scientific evidence to date provides only little support for such recommendations.
Experimental studies that manipulate evening smartphone use are scarce and yield both positive effects of smartphone abstinence as well as null-effects (große Deters et al., 2026).
text.formatted: Experimental studies that manipulate evening smartphone use are scarce and yield both positive effects of smartphone abstinence as well as null-effects <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">(große Deters et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: Moreover, they face several methodological challenges, including difficulties in recruiting and retaining participants and the potential for expectancy effects (große Deters et al., 2026).
text.formatted: Moreover, they face several methodological challenges, including difficulties in recruiting and retaining participants and the potential for expectancy effects <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">(große Deters et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: Intensive longitudinal studies offer an important complementary approach to experimental work by examining withinperson associations over time.

However, they also remain relatively rare and their mixed findings -with some effects even pointing to a beneficial effect of evening smartphone use -question recommendations to refrain from smartphone use (Decorte et al., 2026; große Deters et al., 2026; Tkaczyk et al., 2023).
text.formatted: However, they also remain relatively rare and their mixed findings -with some effects even pointing to a beneficial effect of evening smartphone use -question recommendations to refrain from smartphone use <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">(Decorte et al., 2026;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">große Deters et al., 2026;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b45">Tkaczyk et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: Only cross-sectional research consistently links greater smartphone use to poorer sleep outcomes (Brautsch et al., 2023; Carter et al., 2016; Chu et al., 2023).
text.formatted: Only cross-sectional research consistently links greater smartphone use to poorer sleep outcomes <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">(Brautsch et al., 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">Carter et al., 2016;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">Chu et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: However, such between-person associations may reflect stable individual differences and other confounding factors rather than a causal link between evening smartphone use and sleep.
Individuals who use their smartphones extensively may differ from those who use them less extensively in numerous characteristics that are also related to sleep.
Current recommendations to reduce evening smartphone use should be questioned not only due to the limited and mixed empirical evidence but also on theoretical grounds.

Several mechanisms have been proposed through which evening smartphone use may affect sleep, with some predicting detrimental effects and others suggesting potential benefits (Bauducco et al., 2024; Cain & Gradisar, 2010; große Deters et al., 2026).
text.formatted: Several mechanisms have been proposed through which evening smartphone use may affect sleep, with some predicting detrimental effects and others suggesting potential benefits <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(Bauducco et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">Cain & Gradisar, 2010;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">große Deters et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: Moreover, the temporal dynamics of potential associations between evening smartphone use and sleep remain unclear.
The proposed mechanisms do not clearly indicate when smartphone use should be most consequential.

Existing studies have examined smartphone use in different time windows, but they also differ in numerous other methodological characteristics, making it difficult to integrate their findings and draw reliable and action-guiding conclusions.
The present study aims to contribute much-needed empirical evidence to the existing literature on evening smartphone use and sleep.
We provide a systematic assessment using an intensive longitudinal design with devicebased measures of smartphone use among healthy adults.
To assess the robustness of the findings, we examine the same associations in two samples, providing a within-study replication.
Moreover, we systematically test associations across different pre-sleep time windows to examine whether the timing of smartphone use relative to shuteye timefoot_0 matters.
text.formatted: Moreover, we systematically test associations across different pre-sleep time windows to examine whether the timing of smartphone use relative to shuteye time<ref type="foot" target="#foot_0">foot_0</ref> matters.

text.text: The most direct way to test whether reducing evening smartphone use improves sleep is to experimentally manipulate smartphone use.

However, only very few studies have done so, and their findings are mixed: some reported significant improvements in sleep following restrictions of smartphone use, whereas others found no significant effects (Bartel et al., 2019; Duraccio et al., 2021; Harris et al., 2015; He et al., 2020; Larsen et al., 2021; Perrault et al., 2019; Shepherd, 2021).
text.formatted: However, only very few studies have done so, and their findings are mixed: some reported significant improvements in sleep following restrictions of smartphone use, whereas others found no significant effects <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">(Bartel et al., 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">Duraccio et al., 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">Harris et al., 2015;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">He et al., 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">Larsen et al., 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">Perrault et al., 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b42">Shepherd, 2021)</ref>.

text.text: In addition to the scarcity and ambiguity of the experimental evidence to date, experimental research in this area faces important methodological challenges.

First, researchers have highlighted substantial difficulties in recruiting participants who are willing to alter their smartphone use (Bartel et al., 2019; Perrault et al., 2019), resulting in samples that are highly prone to self-selection.
text.formatted: First, researchers have highlighted substantial difficulties in recruiting participants who are willing to alter their smartphone use <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">(Bartel et al., 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">Perrault et al., 2019)</ref>, resulting in samples that are highly prone to self-selection.

text.text: As a consequence, many studies are based on relatively small samples, ranging between 33 and 75 participants, and are therefore likely underpowered (for exceptions, see Duraccio et al., 2021; Perrault et al., 2019).
text.formatted: As a consequence, many studies are based on relatively small samples, ranging between 33 and 75 participants, and are therefore likely underpowered (for exceptions, see <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">Duraccio et al., 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">Perrault et al., 2019)</ref>.

text.text: These recruitment challenges are further exacerbated by considerable (selective) dropout rates, which have been reported to range from 24% to 39% (Bartel et al., 2019; Duraccio et al., 2021; Harris et al., 2015; Perrault et al., 2019).
text.formatted: These recruitment challenges are further exacerbated by considerable (selective) dropout rates, which have been reported to range from 24% to 39% <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">(Bartel et al., 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">Duraccio et al., 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">Harris et al., 2015;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">Perrault et al., 2019)</ref>.

text.text: Together, small sample sizes and high (selective) attrition substantially limit the statistical power, validity, and generalizability of the findings.
Second, experiments manipulating evening smartphone use are particularly vulnerable to expectancy effects.
Given the widespread belief that evening smartphone use negatively affects sleep, participants may readily infer the study hypotheses and become aware of what is expected of them (Ferguson, 2024).
text.formatted: Given the widespread belief that evening smartphone use negatively affects sleep, participants may readily infer the study hypotheses and become aware of what is expected of them <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">(Ferguson, 2024)</ref>.

text.text: This awareness may influence their behavior in accordance with these expectations, thereby introducing demand characteristics and placebo-like effects that threaten internal validity (Boot et al., 2013; Orne, 1962).
text.formatted: This awareness may influence their behavior in accordance with these expectations, thereby introducing demand characteristics and placebo-like effects that threaten internal validity <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">(Boot et al., 2013;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">Orne, 1962)</ref>.

text.text: Thus, although experiments offer strong control over the manipulation, their feasibility and validity may be limited in the context of evening smartphone use.
Intensive longitudinal studies repeatedly assess smartphone use and sleep outcomes within the same individuals.

Hence, they allow researchers to examine whether deviations from a person's typical evening smartphone use are associated with corresponding changes in their sleep while eliminating the influence of stable between-person differences.
To date, however, only a few intensive longitudinal studies have examined evening smartphone use and sleep.
The findings are mixed, but notably mostly do not support the assumption that greater-than-usual evening smartphone use is associated with poorer sleep.
One study found a significant negative within-person association between evening smartphone use and sleep quality, but no association with sleep duration (Kühnel et al., 2020).
text.formatted: One study found a significant negative within-person association between evening smartphone use and sleep quality, but no association with sleep duration <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">(Kühnel et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: Several other studies found null associations across all assessed sleep outcomes (Lee et al., 2021; Siebers et al., 2024; Sumter et al., 2024).
text.formatted: Several other studies found null associations across all assessed sleep outcomes <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">(Lee et al., 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">Siebers et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b44">Sumter et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Interestingly, three studies even suggest potentially beneficial associations.

In a 14-day study of 203 adolescents, nights with greater evening smartphone use were characterized by earlier sleep onset and longer sleep duration, whereas no associations emerged for other sleep outcomes, including sleep latency, sleep quality, and daily sleepiness (Tkaczyk et al., 2023).
text.formatted: In a 14-day study of 203 adolescents, nights with greater evening smartphone use were characterized by earlier sleep onset and longer sleep duration, whereas no associations emerged for other sleep outcomes, including sleep latency, sleep quality, and daily sleepiness <ref type="bibr" target="#b45">(Tkaczyk et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: A similar pattern was found in an intensive longitudinal study with 401 adults: evening smartphone use did not significantly predict sleep latency or sleep quality, but greater evening smartphone use was associated with earlier shuteye times and longer sleep duration (große Deters et al., 2026).
text.formatted: A similar pattern was found in an intensive longitudinal study with 401 adults: evening smartphone use did not significantly predict sleep latency or sleep quality, but greater evening smartphone use was associated with earlier shuteye times and longer sleep duration <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">(große Deters et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: And a 14-day longitudinal study based on iPhone screenshots from 68 adults found that longer in-bed smartphone use predicted longer sleep duration (Decorte et al., 2026).
text.formatted: And a 14-day longitudinal study based on iPhone screenshots from 68 adults found that longer in-bed smartphone use predicted longer sleep duration <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">(Decorte et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: Overall, the intensive longitudinal evidence so far provides little indication of a robust detrimental association between evening smartphone use and sleep and the limited number of studies and their heterogeneous findings preclude firm conclusions.
Moreover, previous studies have examined smartphone use across time windows of varying lengths, ranging from 30 minutes to 3 hours before shuteye time.
However, no study has systematically examined whether associations between smartphone use and sleep outcomes vary depending on how close to or far from shuteye time the use occurs.
Or in other words, whether associations between smartphone use and sleep differ across different segments of the evening.
Further research is needed to establish the robustness and replicability of existing findings and to examine potential variation across time windows.
It is also unclear on theoretical grounds whether evening smartphone use should be associated with sleep at all, and, if so, in which direction.

Early research proposed three mechanisms through which evening smartphone use might impair sleep: (1) suppression of melatonin resulting from exposure to (blue) light emitted from screens, (2) increased pre-sleep arousal resulting from engaging or stimulating activities, and (3) smartphone use delaying or displacing sleep (Cain & Gradisar, 2010).
text.formatted: Early research proposed three mechanisms through which evening smartphone use might impair sleep: (1) suppression of melatonin resulting from exposure to (blue) light emitted from screens, (2) increased pre-sleep arousal resulting from engaging or stimulating activities, and (3) smartphone use delaying or displacing sleep <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">(Cain & Gradisar, 2010)</ref>.

text.text: More recently, however, theoretical accounts have highlighted mechanisms through which evening media use may instead facilitate sleep.
The media recovery hypothesis proposes that engaging with media in the evening can foster relaxation and facilitate the transition to sleep (Ellithorpe et al., 2025; Reinecke & Rieger, 2021).
text.formatted: The media recovery hypothesis proposes that engaging with media in the evening can foster relaxation and facilitate the transition to sleep <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">(Ellithorpe et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">Reinecke & Rieger, 2021)</ref>.

text.text: Consistent with this account, evidence from a sample of 684 adolescents indicates that a majority (62%) intentionally turn to technology -most often smartphones -to regulate negative thoughts at bedtime (Daniels et al., 2023).
text.formatted: Consistent with this account, evidence from a sample of 684 adolescents indicates that a majority (62%) intentionally turn to technology -most often smartphones -to regulate negative thoughts at bedtime <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">(Daniels et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: Physiological data provide converging support for a potentially relaxing effect: using wearable cameras alongside heart rate monitoring, Meredith-Jones et al. (2026) found that screen-based activities were associated with lower median heart rates than non-screen activities.
text.formatted: Physiological data provide converging support for a potentially relaxing effect: using wearable cameras alongside heart rate monitoring, <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">Meredith-Jones et al. (2026)</ref> found that screen-based activities were associated with lower median heart rates than non-screen activities.

text.text: Although the study did not distinguish between devices, social media use, a dominant smartphone activity, showed the lowest heart rate levels, suggesting that certain forms of media engagement may be associated with reduced pre-sleep arousal.
Evening smartphone use may also displace other activities that are potentially more disruptive to sleep (große Deters et al., 2026; Tkaczyk et al., 2023).
text.formatted: Evening smartphone use may also displace other activities that are potentially more disruptive to sleep (große <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">Deters et al., 2026;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b45">Tkaczyk et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: For instance, Ellithorpe et al. (2022) found that greater use of "traditional media," such as television, radio, movies, or video games, in the hour before bedtime was associated with shorter sleep duration.
text.formatted: For instance, <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">Ellithorpe et al. (2022)</ref> found that greater use of "traditional media," such as television, radio, movies, or video games, in the hour before bedtime was associated with shorter sleep duration.

text.text: Accordingly, if individuals use their smartphones instead of engaging in other, potentially more timeconsuming or activating activities, this substitution could facilitate an earlier transition to sleep.
Each of these proposed processes is at least partially supported by empirical evidence (Bauducco et al., 2024; große Deters et al., 2026; Tkaczyk et al., 2023).
text.formatted: Each of these proposed processes is at least partially supported by empirical evidence <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(Bauducco et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">große Deters et al., 2026;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b45">Tkaczyk et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: Importantly, however, in daily life these mechanisms are unlikely to operate in isolation.
They may occur simultaneously, interact with one another, or counteract each other.

For example, consistent with the media recovery hypothesis, individuals may turn to their devices to achieve a relaxed state by listening to calming music, watching light entertainment, or engaging in low-effort browsing.
However, they may subsequently encounter activating stimuli, such as urgent work emails or emotionally charged news.

In response, they may continue using their smartphones to downregulate this heightened pre-sleep arousal by seeking distraction, reassurance, or closure, thereby extending smartphone use and potentially displacing or delaying sleep.
Similarly, individuals may use their smartphones to fill time before going to sleep instead of engaging in longer or more activating activities, such as watching a movie or exercising.

While this substitution might facilitate an earlier shuteye time, exposure to short-wavelength light from a smartphone screen held close to the face could simultaneously suppress melatonin and delay physiological readiness for sleep.
Taken together, these considerations suggest that the association between evening smartphone usage and sleep may be more complex than a simple detrimental effect.
The proposed mechanisms may operate simultaneously, interact with one another, or counteract each other.
Hence, the net association may be detrimental, beneficial, or negligible, depending on the balance of the processes involved.
Consequently, although individual mechanisms may predict effects in specific directions, their combined influence on sleep in everyday life is difficult to predict a priori.
This highlights the value of research that examines the overall association between smartphone use and sleep under naturalistic conditions.
It provides evidence that is directly relevant to practical recommendations, such as whether smartphone use should be avoided during specific pre-sleep intervals.

When considering whether evening smartphone use is a worthwhile target for interventions to improve sleep, it is important to consider the possibility that smartphone use during different parts of the evening may have different net effects.
For example, melatonin suppression earlier in the evening may be less consequential because more time remains before sleep.

At the same time, smartphone use may displace more time-consuming media activities, such as watching a movie, potentially resulting in a positive net association between early-evening smartphone use and sleep.

However, the opposite pattern is also plausible: reduced melatonin production earlier in the evening could delay subsequent activities that facilitate winding down, resulting in a negative net association.

Later in the evening, by contrast, the effects of melatonin suppression may be partly offset by already elevated homeostatic sleep pressure according to the two process model of sleep regulation (Borbély, 1982).
text.formatted: Later in the evening, by contrast, the effects of melatonin suppression may be partly offset by already elevated homeostatic sleep pressure according to the two process model of sleep regulation <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">(Borbély, 1982)</ref>.

text.text: Taken together, these considerations illustrate the complexity of the underlying processes and underscore the need to empirically assess whether and how the association between evening smartphone use and sleep varies across the evening.
A recent study systematically assessed the association of evening smartphone use in the time windows of 30, 60, 120, and 180 minutes before shuteye time (große Deters et al., 2026).
text.formatted: A recent study systematically assessed the association of evening smartphone use in the time windows of 30, 60, 120, and 180 minutes before shuteye time <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">(große Deters et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: These windows were nested and each longer window included the smartphone use captured by the shorter windows.
Significant associations of more evening smartphone use with earlier shuteye time and longer sleep duration were slightly more pronounced for shorter time windows.
If effects of smartphone use differ not only in strength but also in direction between different parts of the evening, longer time windows could be expected to result in attenuated effects.
Consequently, differences between the estimates cannot be interpreted as evidence that smartphone use during one particular part of the evening is more strongly associated with sleep outcomes.
Hence, in the present study we test the effects of four time windows of equal length covering different segments of the evening.
The present study aims to contribute thorough empirical evidence to the existing literature.

We used data from a 10-day experience sampling study with couples, which we divided into two samples at the couple level to allow for a within-study replication while avoiding dependencies between partners and retaining all observations.
Participants' smartphone use was captured automatically via mobile sensing, thereby avoiding biases inherent in self-reported smartphone use (große Deters & Schoedel, 2024; Sewall et al., 2020).
text.formatted: Participants' smartphone use was captured automatically via mobile sensing, thereby avoiding biases inherent in self-reported smartphone use <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">(große Deters & Schoedel, 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b41">Sewall et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: We calculated smartphone use across four nonoverlapping 30-minute time windows covering different segments of the 2-hour period preceding shuteye time and assessed its associations with the sleep-related outcomes shuteye time, sleep duration, sleep latency, difficulties to fall asleep, and sleep quality.
We originally preregistered directional hypotheses predicting negative associations between evening smartphone use and sleep.

However, before beginning the data analyses, additional studies reporting associations in the opposite direction had emerged, along with theoretical mechanisms that could plausibly account for such associations.
We therefore updated our hypotheses and tested them nondirectionally instead.

Ethical approval was granted by the psychology department's ethics committee at (information removed for double-blind peer review), and all procedures were compliant with the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR).

text.text: Due to privacy considerations and compliance with GDPR, the raw smartphone sensing data cannot be publicly shared.
Instead, we provide access to datasets containing the aggregated variables derived during preprocessing, which are used for the reported analyses.

These datasets, together with the R code used for preprocessing, feature extraction, and statistical analyses, are available on Zenodo: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.24109913 (Datasets); https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.24131388 (R Code for Data Processing and Feature Extraction); https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.24131565 (R Code for Statistical Analyses).

text.text: Eligibility for participation required participants to be at least 18 years old, have sufficient proficiency in German, be in a stable romantic relationship of at least six months, and cohabit with their romantic partner (at least across the study period).

Both partners had to be willing to participate and to own a smartphone, with at least one partner using an Android device (version 7 or higher) capable of running the movisensXS app, which measured smartphone use.
Participants received either financial compensation or course credit.

Of the N = 369 included participants, n= 256 were members of 128 couples in which both partners contributed digital trace data, while n = 113 were the sole contributing partner from their couple (due to missing sensing data).
Observations within the n = 256 complete couples, cannot be considered fully independent.
Therefore, the dataset was divided into two separate samples.

Specifically, couples were split up and randomly assigned to either Sample 1 or Sample 2, while participants whose partner was not included in the dataset were randomly allocated to one of the two samples to ensure balanced samples.
Please note that we preregistered to only include one randomly chosen partner per couple, if both partners have smartphone sensing data.
However, we reevaluated this approach before data analyses and decided to rather proceed as described here to retain all data and allow for a within-study replication.
To ensure that extraordinary nights do not bias the results, we applied the following preregistered exclusion criteria on the level of nights.

We excluded nights (1) with a sleep duration of less than 2 hours and more than 16 hours, (2) if the wake-up time was not in the interval between 4 a.m. and 3 p.m., and (3) if the bedtime was not in the interval between 5 p.m. and 5 a.m..
After registering for the study, participants took part in an introductory session led by trained recruiters.
During this session, they received detailed information about the study aims, procedures, and the handling of their data.
Participants who remained interested in taking part were sent informed consent forms, which they read and completed at home.

Those who consented to the mobile sensing component and used an Android smartphone then installed the movisensXS app (http://www.movisens.com/) on their Android smartphones during a second session to allow for the unobtrusive measurement of smartphone use.
text.formatted: Those who consented to the mobile sensing component and used an Android smartphone then installed the movisensXS app (<ref type="url" target="http://www.movisens.com/">www.movisens.com</ref>) on their Android smartphones during a second session to allow for the unobtrusive measurement of smartphone use.

text.text: To combine smartphone use data and data from the questionnaires, participants' pseudonymous identifiers were entered into the administrative backend of formR (Arslan et al., 2020), which served to coordinate and automate the ecological momentary assessment (EMA) procedure.
text.formatted: To combine smartphone use data and data from the questionnaires, participants' pseudonymous identifiers were entered into the administrative backend of formR <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">(Arslan et al., 2020)</ref>, which served to coordinate and automate the ecological momentary assessment (EMA) procedure.

text.text: The smartphone sensing app movisensXS ran in the background, automatically collecting timestamped logs of the events "screen on" and "screen off."
Smartphone use was calculated as the difference between paired screen-on and screen-off events.

We then summed the duration of smartphone use across four non-overlapping 30-minute time windows covering different segments of the 2-hour interval preceding shuteye time: Time Window 1 (0-30 minutes before shuteye time), Time Window 2 (30-60 minutes before shuteye time), Time Window 3 (60-90 minutes before shuteye time), and Time Window 4 (90-120 minutes before shuteye time).
Self-reported shuteye time was used to calculate these time windows for each individual and evening.

We preregistered rules for handling potential logging errors and set smartphone use to missing if more than 5 minutes within a given time window consisted of "missing time" -defined as periods during which smartphone use or non-use could not be reliably determined from the recorded data.
For more details on this process, please refer to the Appendix.
Descriptive statistics are reported in Table 1, and repeated-measures correlations (within-person associations) among study variables are presented in Table 2.
text.formatted: Descriptive statistics are reported in Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_0">1</ref>, and repeated-measures correlations (within-person associations) among study variables are presented in Table <ref type="table">2</ref>.

text.text: During the 10 days following the installation of the sensing app, participants received six EMA prompts per day between 09:30 and 21:30.
The first five prompts were semi-randomly scheduled throughout the day with a minimum interval of 50 minutes between consecutive prompts, whereas the final prompt was always sent at 21:30.

Surveys remained accessible for 30 minutes following the first five prompts and for 60 minutes following the final prompt; once started, they had to be completed within 10 and 30 minutes, respectively.

Sleep outcomes were measured in the first survey that participants started on a given day (e.g., if participants missed the first prompt of the day, the sleep-related items were presented in the second survey).
Participants reported their sleep latency by answering the item "How long do you think it took you to fall asleep?
This refers to the time between switching off the light and falling asleep (i.e. the time when you intended to fall asleep; not reading or using your mobile phone)".
They also indicated their sleep onset time ("I fell asleep last night at the following time:") and their wake-up time ("I woke up this morning at the following time:").
Sleep duration was then calculated from sleep onset and wake-up time and shuteye time was derived by subtracting sleep latency from sleep onset time.

To address potential inaccuracies in the self-reports and to ensure that exceptional nights do not skew the analyses, we preregistered and implemented some corrections, like setting sleep duration to missing if self-reported wake-up time was before self-reported sleep onset time (see Appendix for a full list of corrections).

Participants indicated on a 7-point rating scale their sleep quality ("How did you sleep last night?", scale: very poorly -very well) as well as their difficulties to fall asleep "Did you find it difficult to fall asleep last night?", scale: not at all -very much).
To facilitate interpretation, sleep quality and difficulties to fall asleep were both linearly transformed into POMP scores (percentage of maximum possible; Cohen et al., 1999).
text.formatted: To facilitate interpretation, sleep quality and difficulties to fall asleep were both linearly transformed into POMP scores (percentage of maximum possible; <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">Cohen et al., 1999)</ref>.

text.text: Scores range from 0 to 100, providing a more intuitive metric that is independent of sample-specific characteristics.

text.text: To determine whether a night preceded a working or non-working day, we used participants' responses to an item in the following day's evening questionnaire assessing work hours ("How many hours did you work today?
If you did not work, enter 0 hours.").
Specifically, reporting zero hours was coded as 0 (non-working day), more than zero hours as 1 (working day), and no entry as missing.
In line with our preregistration, we fitted linear multilevel models predicting sleep outcomes (Level 1) from evening smartphone use assessed at the same level.

This approach appropriately accounts for the hierarchical structure of the data, with repeated observations nested within individuals, and allows for the estimation of withinperson associations (Nezlek, 2008).
text.formatted: This approach appropriately accounts for the hierarchical structure of the data, with repeated observations nested within individuals, and allows for the estimation of withinperson associations <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">(Nezlek, 2008)</ref>.

text.text: All Level 1-predictors were person-mean centered (i.e., centered within cluster).
We used the lme4 package (version 2.0-6; Bates et al., 2015) in R (version 4.5.1; R Core Team, 2025) for model estimation.
text.formatted: We used the lme4 package (version 2.0-6; <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">Bates et al., 2015)</ref> in R (version 4.5.1; R Core Team, 2025) for model estimation.

text.text: We ran separate models for each combination of the four 30-minute time windows of evening smartphone use and the five sleep outcomes (shuteye time, sleep duration, sleep latency, difficulties to fall asleep, and sleep quality) in each of our two samples, yielding a total of 40 models.
Following recommendations, we initially specified models with a maximal random effects structure, including random slopes (Barr et al., 2013).
text.formatted: Following recommendations, we initially specified models with a maximal random effects structure, including random slopes <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(Barr et al., 2013)</ref>.

text.text: However, these models failed to converge, and -as preregistered -we then simplified the random effects structure.
Inspection of model diagnostics revealed deviations from normality in the residuals for sleep latency in both samples.
To address this issue, we added 1 to sleep latency to accommodate zero values and then log-transformed the resulting variable before fitting the models.
All remaining outcomes were analyzed using Gaussian models with an identity link function.
We further tested whether associations between evening smartphone use and sleep outcomes differed depending on whether the respective night preceded a working day.
To this end, both the main effect of working day and its interaction with evening smartphone use (person-mean centered) were included in the models.

text.text: Across time windows and samples, longer evening smartphone use was consistently associated with earlier shuteye times.
And in all but two models these associations were statistically significant.
With regard to the magnitude of the association, using the smartphone 10 minutes longer than usual within a 30-minute time window was associated with a 3.8-to 8.7minute earlier shuteye time.
In respect to differences between the four time windows, inspection of the effect sizes across both samples provided no indication that any particular time window was more relevant than the others.
Nor was there a systematic pattern suggesting that effects became larger or smaller as the time window was closer to shuteye time.
Interestingly, while longer evening smartphone use was associated with earlier shuteye times, this did not translate into equally robust effects on sleep duration.
While longer smartphone use was associated with longer sleep duration -apart from one exception -only one effect reached significance.
In terms of effect size, a 10-minute increase in smartphone use in comparison to their usual evening smartphone use was associated with 2.4 minutes shorter to 5.2 minutes longer sleep duration.
We log-transformed sleep latency after adding one minute to accommodate self-reports of zero sleep latency.

Consequently, the interpretation of the coefficients differs from that of the models for other outcomes: A positive coefficient for smartphone use indicates a multiplicative increase in sleep latency plus one.

For instance, within Time Window 1 for Sample 1, each additional minute of smartphone use is associated with a predicted increase in sleep latency + 1 by a factor of exp(0.005)=1.005, corresponding to an approximately 0.5 % increase
For sleep latency, longer evening smartphone use was consistently associated with participants taking slightly longer to fall asleep.
However, 5 out of 8 effects were non-significant, the few significant effects did not replicate across samples, and all effects were tiny.

To illustrate the small magnitude of the effects, a 10-minute increase in smartphone use was associated with 10-51 seconds longer sleep latency for participants who usually take 16 minutes to fall asleep 2 .
For the outcomes sleep quality and difficulties to fall asleep null effects emerged.
Across time windows and samples, evening smartphone use showed very small and non-significant associations with these outcomes.

In order to test whether associations between evening smartphone use and sleep outcomes differed depending on whether the respective night preceded a working day or a non-working day, we added both the main effect of type of day and its interaction with evening smartphone use to the models.
All results of these analyses can be found in the Appendix (Tables A1-A5).
text.formatted: All results of these analyses can be found in the Appendix (Tables <ref type="table" target="#tab_0">A1-A5</ref>).

text.text: For shuteye time, unsurprisingly, day type was a significant predictor, with earlier shuteye times on nights preceding a working day.
The associations between evening smartphone use and shuteye time remained negative and similar in magnitude for both working and non-working days.
The effects of evening smartphone use before working days mostly reached significance while almost all associations of evening smartphone use before non-working days were non-significant.
However, none of the interaction effects was statistically significant, and the interaction estimates showed no consistent direction across samples and time windows.
Thus, there was no evidence of systematic moderation by working day.
Sleep duration was shorter on nights preceding working days, although this effect did not reach statistical significance consistently.
The associations between evening smartphone use and sleep duration remained mostly positive, similar in size, and non-significant.
Again, none of the interaction effects was statistically significant, and their estimates varied in direction, providing no evidence of moderation by day type.
For sleep latency, sleep quality, and difficulties to fall asleep, day type showed no consistent associations, and none of the effects reached statistical significance.
The main effects of evening smartphone use were very similar to those observed in models without day type.
Moreover, the interaction effects provided no indication that associations 2 Because of the +1 transformation, the estimated effect on the original scale depends on the assumed sleep latency.
To illustrate the effect size, we assumed a sleep latency of 16 minutes which corresponds to the average sleep latency reported in Sample 1.
The range of 10-51 seconds was calculated by back-transforming the regression coefficients from log(sleep latency + 1) to the original scale using (16+1)×[exp(10β)-1].
between evening smartphone use and these sleep outcomes differed depending on day type.
Interaction estimates varied in direction across samples and time windows and were almost uniformly non-significant, with two exceptions that did not replicate across samples.

In line with previous intensive longitudinal research, we found no robust evidence pointing to a harmful effect of evening smartphone use on sleep (Decorte et al., 2026; große Deters et al., 2026; Kühnel et al., 2020; Lee et al., 2021; Siebers et al., 2024; Sumter et al., 2024; Tkaczyk et al., 2023).
