text.text: Instead, contrary to the widespread belief that smartphone use delays sleep, greater-than-usual evening smartphone use was consistently associated with earlier shuteye times across all time windows and in both samples.
Interestingly, the only other intensive longitudinal study that examined shuteye time found the same effect (große Deters et al., 2026).
text.formatted: Interestingly, the only other intensive longitudinal study that examined shuteye time found the same effect <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">(große Deters et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: In this study, using a smartphone for 10 minutes longer than usual during the 30-minute period directly preceding shuteye time (comparable to Time Window 1 in the present study) was associated with a 6.7-minute earlier shuteye time.
In our study, the corresponding associations were 6.1 and 3.9 minutes earlier shuteye time in Samples 1 and 2, respectively.
To put the size of these effects into context, shuteye times differed for participants by 17 minutes between evenings preceding working days and evenings preceding non-working days.
Hence, a 4-7-minute difference associated with just 10 minutes more smartphone use should be considered a substantial effect.

In terms of robustness, our findings were less stable than those reported by große Deters et al. ( 2026) whose effects remained consistent in both direction and statistical significance after accounting for working versus nonworking days.
text.formatted: In terms of robustness, our findings were less stable than those reported by große Deters et al. ( <ref type="formula">2026</ref>) whose effects remained consistent in both direction and statistical significance after accounting for working versus nonworking days.

text.text: Although we found -just as große Deters et al. ( 2026) -no evidence of systematic moderation by working day, the simple slopes for evenings preceding non-working days were predominantly not statistically significant.
text.formatted: Although we found -just as große Deters et al. ( <ref type="formula">2026</ref>) -no evidence of systematic moderation by working day, the simple slopes for evenings preceding non-working days were predominantly not statistically significant.

text.text: This reduction in statistical significance for non-working days should be interpreted in the context of the unequal number of observations across day types, as well as the loss of 24% of evenings in Sample 1 and 28% in Sample 2 due to missing values on the working-day variable, which may have reduced statistical power and precision.

Descriptively, greater evening smartphone use than usual was predominantly associated with longer sleep duration, which again is consistent with findings from three previous studies (Decorte et al., 2026; große Deters et al., 2026; Tkaczyk et al., 2023).
text.formatted: Descriptively, greater evening smartphone use than usual was predominantly associated with longer sleep duration, which again is consistent with findings from three previous studies <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">(Decorte et al., 2026;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">große Deters et al., 2026;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b45">Tkaczyk et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: However, in the present study, most of these associations did not reach statistical significance.
For sleep latency, greater-than-usual evening smartphone use was associated with slightly longer sleep latency -but mostly the association was not significant and never replicated across samples.
Considering the size of the effect:
A 10-minute increase in smartphone use was associated with 10-51 seconds longer sleep latency among participants who typically took 16 minutes to fall asleep.
For comparison, a meta-analysis of 19 studies found that caffeine consumption versus no caffein consumption increased sleep onset latency by approximately 9 minutes (Gardiner et al., 2023).
text.formatted: For comparison, a meta-analysis of 19 studies found that caffeine consumption versus no caffein consumption increased sleep onset latency by approximately 9 minutes <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">(Gardiner et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: Thus, even at the upper end of the observed range, the associations between smartphone use and sleep latency were very small in absolute terms.

Taken together, the lack of replication across samples and the small magnitude of the associations provide little evidence for a robust or practically meaningful relationship between evening smartphone use and sleep latency.

In previous longitudinal studies associations between evening smartphone use and sleep latency were also small and not significant (große Deters et al., 2026; Sumter et al., 2024; Tkaczyk et al., 2023).
text.formatted: In previous longitudinal studies associations between evening smartphone use and sleep latency were also small and not significant <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">(große Deters et al., 2026;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b44">Sumter et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b45">Tkaczyk et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: With regard to timing, we found no indication that smartphone use during different segments of the evening is systematically differently associated with sleep.

Differences in the estimated effects between the two samples were comparable in magnitude to differences across time windows, suggesting that the observed variation may largely reflect sampling variability rather than a systematic effect of timing.

Likewise, no temporal pattern across time windows could be detected: associations did not consistently become stronger or weaker as the time window approached shuteye time, nor did the windows closest to or furthest from shuteye time show systematically stronger, weaker or differently directed effects.
Interestingly, within-person correlations of smartphone use across different time windows were only moderate, with correlations between neighboring time windows ranging from .36 to .44.
Thus, individuals did not have evenings characterized by consistently higher or lower smartphone use; rather, the amount of smartphone use varied across different segments of the same evening.
However, averaged across all individuals and days, smartphone use was largely the same for each of the four time windows with means of around 8 minutes and medians around 5 minutes.
Our results have important implications both for the interpretation of previous as well as the planning of future research.

Previous intensive longitudinal studies and experiments have focused on a range of time windows, from 30 minutes to 3 hours before bedtime or shuteye time, as well as broader periods such as from 7 p.m. until sleep onset, and restrictions on smartphone use in the bedroom.

That the pattern of effects remained the same across all segments of the evening in our study suggests that differences in the direction of effects between these previous studies are unlikely to be explained by heterogeneity in time windows.
In respect to future research, experimental studies remain important for establishing causal effects and ruling out potential confounding factors at the situational level.
Our findings may inform the design of such studies and help to choose a "manipulation window".
Actual shuteye time varies considerably across evenings (Md within-person SD = 49.6/43.9 minutes in Sample 1/Sample 2) and may be affected by smartphone usage.

If participants are instructed to change their smartphone usage in a time window too close to participants' typical shuteye time, on some evenings they may already have stopped using their smartphones simply because they are preparing for sleep, instead than in response to the manipulation.
In a no-use condition, this could inflate apparent adherence on evenings when participants go to sleep earlier than usual.

Although this would not necessarily bias estimates of the effect of assignment to the experimental condition in a randomized experiment, it could complicate the interpretation of adherence and estimates of the effects of actually following the manipulation.

Our findings showing similar effects across different segments of the evening indicate that the manipulation of smartphone usage could be implemented during a time window that precedes typical shuteye time by a sufficient margin.

Scheduling the manipulation sufficiently before typical shuteye time may help distinguish naturally occurring reductions in smartphone use from reductions attributable to the experimental manipulation.
Taken together, our study provides robust and comprehensive evidence that advances the growing body of intensive longitudinal research on the relationship between evening smartphone use and sleep.

In line with previous literature, our findings caution against assuming that evening smartphone use has detrimental effects on sleep, point to an even potentially beneficial association with shuteye time and add important insights on temporal aspects of the associations between evening smartphone use and sleep.
An important limitation of the present study is its observational nature as we cannot establish causal relationships.
Compared with cross-sectional designs, our intensive longitudinal approach offers the important advantage of accounting for stable between-person differences.
Nevertheless, the observed associations may still reflect confounding by time-varying situational factors.

For example, an alternative explanation for the observed association between greater-than-usual smartphone use and earlier shuteye time is that, following a more strenuous day, individuals may find it more difficult to regulate their smartphone use, potentially contributing to prolonged use.
At the same time, greater fatigue may prompt them to go to bed earlier.
Thus, the observed association could reflect the influence of a common situational factor rather than a direct relationship between smartphone use and shuteye time.

As outlined in the introduction, experimental studies -the gold standard for establishing causality -face two main challenges in this research area: (1) recruiting and retaining participants willing to reduce their smartphone use and (2) potential bias due to expectancy effects, given the widespread assumption that smartphone use is detrimental to sleep.
Because establishing causality remains essential, we suggest several approaches for future experimental research.

First, with the present study adding further null findings and evidence of beneficial associations between evening smartphone use and sleep to the existing body of literature, the research question could now be framed explicitly as an open empirical question rather than as a test of an assumed detrimental effect.
Communicating the current state of the evidence to participants before the study may help reduce expectancy effects by challenging their pre-existing assumptions.

Second, because self-reported sleep outcomes may be particularly susceptible to expectancy effects, future experimental studies should complement self-report measures with device-based assessments of sleep.
Combining subjective and objective measures would help distinguish changes in perceived sleep from changes in objectively assessed sleep parameters.

Third, given the current state of the evidence, experimental studies could consider manipulating evening smartphone use in either direction, including instructing participants to increase their use rather than abstain from it.

As smartphones serve a wide range of everyday functions, such an intervention may be less burdensome for participants, potentially facilitating recruitment, improving adherence, and reducing attrition.
Beyond its observational design, another limitation of the present study is its focus on overall smartphone use at the device level.
Smartphones serve a wide range of functions, and the implications of their use for sleep may depend on the specific applications used and activities performed.
Although screen light exposure is common across most types of app use, other potential mechanisms may depend on the nature of the activity.

For example, apps designed to promote relaxation might reduce pre-sleep arousal and thereby benefit sleep (Flett et al., 2019), whereas interactive games might have the opposite effect (Reinecke et al., 2011).
text.formatted: For example, apps designed to promote relaxation might reduce pre-sleep arousal and thereby benefit sleep <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">(Flett et al., 2019)</ref>, whereas interactive games might have the opposite effect <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">(Reinecke et al., 2011)</ref>.

text.text: Future research should therefore move beyond overall use duration to examine whether specific apps, activities, or use patterns are differentially associated with sleep outcomes.

Last but not least, our samples consisted of highly educated couples who shared relational contexts and potentially overlapping social environments, and who agreed to have their smartphone use monitored.
Future research needs to establish the generalizability of our results to other populations.
The present study questions widespread assumptions and recommendations to abstain from evening smartphone use in order to improve sleep.
The current evidence on the relationship between evening smartphone use and sleep is not yet conclusive, and as an important next step, particularly studies that allow causal inferences are needed.
Nevertheless, based on the available literature, it is not unreasonable to expect either a null effect or even a net effect in the opposite direction from that commonly assumed.
Importantly, recommendations to change behavior are not without costs when the targeted behavior has no, or only a negligible, effect on health and well-being.

Because changing habits can be difficult and requires sustained effort, encouraging individuals to focus on reducing smartphone use may divert limited self-regulatory resources from other behavioral changes that could have more meaningful effects on health and well-being (Kwasnicka et al., 2016).
text.formatted: Because changing habits can be difficult and requires sustained effort, encouraging individuals to focus on reducing smartphone use may divert limited self-regulatory resources from other behavioral changes that could have more meaningful effects on health and well-being <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">(Kwasnicka et al., 2016)</ref>.

text.text: Moreover, given the consistent within-person associations observed in our study, whereby greater evening smartphone use was associated with earlier shuteye times, blanket recommendations to abstain from smartphone use in the evening could potentially be counterproductive if these associations reflect a causal effect.
At a minimum, the current evidence does not provide a sufficiently strong basis for recommending evening smartphone abstinence as a strategy to improve sleep.
